title: Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Deterministic Verifier Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configuration Changes — Non‑informative Result under Shared‑Generation Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment that evaluated whether a deterministic verifier pipeline (generate → deterministic_netops_validator_v5 → optional repair) reduces the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe intent→configuration proposals produced by a hosted LLM on synthetic NetOps tasks. Design: N=200 preregistered unique tasks in a paired design comparing (a) baseline LLM‑only and (b) a guarded pipeline (declared model gpt‑5‑mini + deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution used shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (independent_condition_generation = false), producing one LLM generation per task shared across arms (model_calls_used = 200; preregistered maximum_model_calls = 400; completed_episode_count = 400; failed_episode_count = 0). Observed (adversarial cluster): baseline SAFE = 200/200; guarded SAFE = 200/200 (paired contingency n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0). Estimated paired SAFE‑rate difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). Because identical per‑pair generations were produced and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis (that a verifier reduces unsafe proposals) was not testable in this run. The paper publishes the complete preregistered run, diagnoses why it was non‑informative, and provides artifact‑anchored recommendations—(1) independent per‑arm generation budgeting (requires model_calls ≈ 400 for N=200), (2) calibrated adversarial injections, and (3) exploratory ROC budgeting—to produce an informative repeat. All execution and analysis artifacts cited here are archived in the supplied bundle (see execution/* and analysis/* paths).

sections.introduction: LLM‑assisted intent→configuration translation promises to reduce operator workload in network operations (NetOps) but raises safety concerns: an incorrect or ill‑timed change can break reachability, violate access policies, or cause outages. Prior work proposes grounding LLMs with deterministic validators, sandboxed replay, and generate–validate–repair loops to reduce constraint violations and hallucinations. To move beyond feasibility demonstrations we preregistered a confirmatory paired experiment (cand‑2026‑01‑prereg‑v1) that asked: How does deterministic tool‑augmentation (generate → deterministic verifier → optional repair) change the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe proposals produced by a hosted LLM under benign and adversarial prompts? We selected a paired binary estimand (guarded minus baseline SAFE‑rate) because it isolates within‑task variance while controlling task difficulty. Contributions: (1) a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment comparing an LLM baseline and a verifier‑augmented pipeline on N=200 synthetic NetOps tasks; (2) an artifact‑grounded diagnosis explaining why the executed run was non‑informative for the preregistered causal estimand; and (3) concrete, quantified recommendations (generation semantics, adversarial budgeting, and model_call accounting) for an informative repeat. All inputs, raw outputs, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are archived (examples: execution/model_configuration.json, execution/execution_manifest.json, execution/raw_results.jsonl, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv).
sections.related_work: Surveys and prototype reports document growing LLM use in NetOps (intent translation, configuration synthesis, and AIOps co‑pilots) and recommend verifier or tool‑augmented pipelines to improve correctness and reduce hallucination risk [1–3]. Empirical and method proposals show that generate–validate–repair architectures can reduce constraint violations in controlled evaluations, though effect sizes depend on verifier fidelity and evaluation semantics [4,5]. Red‑teaming and guardrail literature emphasize a safety–utility trade‑off (false refusals vs. prevented errors) and advocate workflow‑centred, sandboxed, replayable evaluation[2,6]. Our study follows these prescriptions by preregistering a paired design, using a deterministic task generator and validator, and archiving complete validator traces. Unlike many prototypes, we freeze an estimand and budget before execution and publish raw model outputs and deterministic analysis artifacts so other researchers can deterministically replay and probe the run.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and primary estimand: The preregistration (cand‑2026‑01‑prereg‑v1) defined the primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (SAFE encoded as 1) using a paired binary design with N=200 unique tasks (planned_episode_count = 400). The power plan targeted detecting ≈7 percentage‑point paired reductions (baseline ≈12–15% → guarded ≈5%) with 80% power; the computation recommended n≈174 and preregistered N=200 to allow replacements. The preregistration, sampling rules, seeds, and analysis plan were frozen before any model calls and are archived with the run.
sections.results: Confirmatory outcomes (adversarial cluster as preregistered): every confirmatory paired episode was labeled SAFE by the deterministic validator in both arms. Analysis artifacts record baseline_success_count = 200/200 and guarded_success_count = 200/200, giving contingency n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). The paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] using 10,000 resamples with seed = 1729 (analysis artifacts archived). Execution accounting: completed_episode_count = 400, model_calls_used = 200, failed_episode_count = 0 (execution/execution_manifest.json). No verifier refusals or repairs occurred in the confirmatory episodes: repair_provider_trace entries are null in execution/scoring/*.json; validator_traces show validation_before/after with violation_count = 0 per episode.
sections.discussion: Methodological diagnosis (artifact‑grounded): three preregistered/executed choices combined to make the causal test uninformative. (A) Generation semantics: the run executed independent_condition_generation = false (shared_initial_candidate), so each task received a single LLM candidate that was scored under both baseline and guarded arms. This semantic is recorded in execution/model_configuration.json and the execution manifest. (B) Model behavior and adversarial coverage: for the sampled tasks and adversarial prompt templates used in this run, the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) produced candidates that passed the deterministic validator; the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%. (C) Model‑call budgeting: because generations were shared, model_calls_used = 200 while the preregistered maximum_model_calls intended to support independent per‑arm generation was 400. Together these facts created a ceiling effect: identical per‑pair outputs and zero baseline errors make paired discordance impossible and remove statistical power to detect a verifier benefit. Concrete artifact‑anchored recommendations for informative repeats: (1) Use independent per‑arm generation (independent_condition_generation = true). For N=200 this requires model_calls ≈ 400 (one independent generation per arm per task); the difference between executed model_calls_used (200) and preregistered maximum_model_calls (400) quantifies the additional generation budget required. (2) Increase adversarial strength via templated obfuscations and reserve a calibrated exploratory set (preregistered reserve up to 50 tasks) to estimate verifier ROC and refusal rates with CI reporting. (3) Consider modest multi‑model panels to assess generality across model families. Operational implication: deterministic validators are promising guardrails, but demonstrating measurable benefit requires evaluation conditions that yield nonzero baseline error rates and per‑arm output variability. Threats to validity and practical constraints are detailed below.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully archived, preregistered paired experiment comparing an LLM baseline and a deterministic verifier‑augmented pipeline on 200 synthetic NetOps tasks. Under the executed shared_generation semantics (one LLM candidate shared per pair) and for gpt‑5‑mini, both arms produced zero verifier‑detected unsafe proposals (paired difference = 0.0; p = 1.0). Consequently the preregistered causal hypothesis (that a verifier reduces unsafe proposals) was not testable in this run. The main scientific contribution is methodological and reproducibility‑oriented: (1) we publish a deterministically replayable artifact bundle that captures the full preregistered workflow and results (execution/*, analysis/*, scoring JSONs); (2) we identify and quantify how generation semantics and model_call budgeting determine testability; and (3) we provide concrete, artifact‑anchored guidance (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial injection design, exploratory ROC accounting) required to produce an informative repeat. The archived artifacts permit exact deterministic replays and serve as a reusable evaluation template for workflow‑centred NetOps studies.

limitations: Synthetic tasks and scope: tasks were deterministic synthetic topologies limited to single‑AS, multi‑device setups produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; results may not generalize to production, multi‑AS, or vendor‑specific features.

Generation semantics: the executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical per‑pair generations and creating a ceiling effect when shared candidates were valid.

Adversarial strength: the preregistered adversarial templates used in this run did not elicit unsafe outputs from gpt‑5‑mini on the sampled tasks; stronger adversarial cases are required to measure verifier effect.
Single‑model scope: only the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was evaluated; no multi‑model generality is claimed.
Verifier completeness: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 ran deterministically in a synthetic sandbox; a complete match to all real‑world NetOps failure modes is not claimed.

Operational external validity: no production deployment, operator‑in‑the‑loop workload measurement, nor multi‑vendor field trials were performed; operator‑cost trade‑offs remain unquantified at scale.
